parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Define the $moment$ of a force about a point.

markscheme_points.text: force × perpendicular distance (of line of action of force)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what makes a force cause turning - it is not just how big the force is, but also how far from the pivot its line of action passes.
parts.proper_answer: Moment = force $\times$ perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What moment means**
Think of opening a door. Pushing near the hinge hardly turns it, pushing far from the hinge turns it easily. So the turning effect depends on two things together: the size of the force $F$ and how far away it acts.

Step 2: **Why perpendicular matters**
Only the distance measured at $90^{\circ}$ to the force line counts. In symbols: $$ \text{moment} = F \times d_{\perp} $$ where $d_{\perp}$ is the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the SI base units of the moment of a force.

markscheme_points.text: units: kg m s⁻² m = kg m² s⁻²

hints: Hint 1: Start from your definition in (a)(i): moment is a force times a distance, so first write the newton $\text{N}$ in base units $\text{kg}$, $\text{m}$, $\text{s}$ and then multiply by a metre.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Break the newton into base units**
From $F = ma$, force has units of mass $\times$ acceleration: $$ 1\text{ N} = 1\text{ kg} \times 1\text{ m s}^{-2} = 1\text{ kg m s}^{-2} $$

Step 2: **Multiply by distance**
Moment = force $\times$ distance, so: $$ \text{unit of moment} = \text{kg m s}^{-2} \times \text{m} = \text{kg m}^{2}\text{ s}^{-2} $$ This uses only the base units $\text{kg}$, $\text{m}$, $\text{s}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A uniform rigid rod of length $2.4\text{ m}$ is shown in Fig. 1.1.

{{figure:figure_1_1}}

Fig. 1.1

The rod has a weight of $5.2\text{ N}$ and is made of wood of density $790\text{ kg m}^{-3}$.

Calculate the cross-sectional area $A$, in $\text{mm}^2$, of the rod.
hints: Hint 1: Link the given weight and density together through mass - density needs mass and volume, and weight gives you mass if you use $W = mg$.
Hint 2: Write the volume of the uniform rod as area $\times$ length, so $W = \rho A L g$, then rearrange to make $A$ the subject before putting numbers in.
Hint 3: Calculate $A$ in $\text{m}^{2}$ first, then remember $1\text{ m}^{2} = 10^{6}\text{ mm}^{2}$ to convert to $\text{mm}^{2}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Connect weight to density**
You know weight $W = 5.2\text{ N}$, length $L = 2.4\text{ m}$ and density $\rho = 790\text{ kg m}^{-3}$. Density is mass per volume, $\rho = m/V$, and $W = mg$. For a uniform rod of cross-section $A$: $$ V = AL $$ so $$ W = mg = \rho V g = \rho A L g $$

Step 2: **Rearrange and calculate in SI**
Make $A$ the subject: $$ A = \frac{W}{\rho L g} $$ Put numbers in with $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$: $$ A = \frac{5.2}{790 \times 2.4 \times 9.81} \approx 2.8 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^{2} $$

Step 3: **Convert to mm2**
$1\text{ m} = 1000\text{ mm}$, so $1\text{ m}^{2} = (1000)^{2}\text{ mm}^{2} = 10^{6}\text{ mm}^{2}$: $$ A = 2.8 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{6} = 2.8 \times 10^{2}\text{ mm}^{2} $$ about $280\text{ mm}^{2}$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A fishing rod AB, made from the rod in (b), is shown in Fig. 1.2.

{{figure:figure_1_2}}

Fig. 1.2 (not to scale)

End A of the rod rests on the ground and a string is attached to the other end B. A support stick exerts a force perpendicular to the rod at point C. The weight of the rod acts at point D.

The tension $T$ in the string is in a direction perpendicular to the rod. The rod is in equilibrium and inclined at an angle of $56^{\circ}$ to the vertical.

The forces and the distances along the rod of points A, B, C and D are shown in Fig. 1.2.
parts.text: Show that the component of the weight that is perpendicular to the rod is $4.3\text{ N}$.
hints: Hint 1: Draw the vertical weight arrow at D and the rod direction - the angle between the weight (vertical) and the rod is $34^{\circ}$, or use the given $56^{\circ}$ to the vertical to pick sin or cos for the perpendicular part.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Resolve at right angles to the rod**
Weight acts vertically down, but the rod is tilted $56^{\circ}$ to the vertical. The component at $90^{\circ}$ to the rod is the side of the triangle opposite the $56^{\circ}$ angle: $$ W_{\perp} = W \sin 56^{\circ} $$

Step 2: **Show the value**
$$ W_{\perp} = 5.2 \times \sin 56^{\circ} \approx 5.2 \times 0.829 = 4.3\text{ N} $$ This is the only part of the weight that gives a moment about A, because the parallel part acts along the rod.

enrichment.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Draw the vertical weight arrow at D and the rod direction - the angle between the weight (vertical) and the rod is $34^{\circ}$, or use the given $56^{\circ}$ to the vertical to pick sin or cos for the perpendicular part.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: By taking moments about end A of the rod, calculate the tension $T$.
hints: Hint 1: Choose A as the pivot so the contact force at A has no moment - list the three perpendicular forces and their distances from A along the rod.
Hint 2: Decide which way each force turns the rod about A: the $4.6\text{ N}$ stick force opposes the weight component and the tension $T$.
Hint 3: Set sum of clockwise moments equal to sum of anticlockwise moments, using $\text{moment} = F \times$ distance from A, then solve for $T$.
parts.proper_answer: Taking moments about A: $T \times 2.4 + 4.3 \times 1.2 = 4.6 \times 1.8$, giving $T = 1.3\text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get distances from A**
From Fig. 1.2 the total length is $2.4\text{ m}$. Point D (weight) is $1.20\text{ m}$ from A. Point C (stick) is $1.20 + 0.60 = 1.80\text{ m}$ from A. Point B (tension) is $2.40\text{ m}$ from A. All three forces are perpendicular to the rod, so moment is simply $F \times$ distance from A.

Step 2: **Apply equilibrium**
For equilibrium the resultant moment about any point is zero. About A: $$ \text{sum of clockwise moments} = \text{sum of anticlockwise moments} $$ The $4.6\text{ N}$ force acts one way, while $T$ and the $4.3\text{ N}$ weight component act the opposite way: $$ (T \times 2.4) + (4.3 \times 1.2) = 4.6 \times 1.8 $$
